description: We are Xixonencs, a four-member team at Space Apps Valencia building Blind Spot. Our prototype compares measured reaction-test performance with users' own estimates to explore gaps in fatigue awareness. We combine web development, data visualization and human-centered design. Our team is already formed; membership is open so our teammates can officially join.
summary:
On long missions astronauts must judge for themselves whether they are fit for a critical task, and fatigue can degrade exactly that judgment. In January 1986, launch console operators eleven hours into their third consecutive night shift misread an error message and drained 18,000 pounds of liquid oxygen from a Shuttle's tank; the Rogers Commission report cites operator fatigue as one of the major contributing factors.

Blind Spot pairs a short reaction test, based on the PVT-B behind the Reaction Self-Test used on the ISS, with one extra question asked before showing the result: how do you think you did? The gap between the estimate and the result is the crew member's blind spot. A crew view turns it into a status and a clear action.

We piloted it during the hackathon itself, treating the event as an analog crew: 190 tests from 112 participants in one weekend. We report what we found, including what we did not find, and how it changed our design.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Blind Spot is a web app that runs on any phone. The user takes a 12-response reaction test (1 to 4 seconds between stimuli; a lapse is a response of 355 ms or more; a response under 100 ms is a false start). Before seeing the result, the user estimates how many lapses they had. The app compares the estimate with the result, and each person only with their own earlier tests.

A crew control view shows each crew member's status in three levels and answers three questions: what is happening, why it matters, and what to do, for example asking for a second check before a critical task.

HOW WE TESTED IT

We turned the hackathon into our experiment. Participants, mentors and volunteers played the test in four time windows from Saturday midday to Sunday morning: 190 tests, 112 participants, 47 of them more than once. All data is anonymous.

WHAT WE FOUND

- After one short night, participants estimated their own lapses reasonably well.

- We detected no decline in reaction speed with hours awake. No tests were taken between 02:00 and 07:00, the circadian low.

- Phone type changed reaction speed by about 8%, more than any fatigue variable.

- Repeating the test improved results, so practice and time awake cannot be separated in our data.

WHAT THIS CHANGED IN THE DESIGN

- Compare each person only with themselves, on the same device.

- Practice tests before fixing a personal baseline.

- Next step: the full 3-minute PVT-B combined with hours awake, and a study that includes the circadian low.

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

Existing tools measure performance. Blind Spot measures whether the person judges their own performance correctly, which matters most when there is no real-time support from Earth.

LIMITATIONS

Observational pilot with volunteers, on personal phones, with a shortened test. One self-report scale changed during the event and is excluded from our conclusions. Health indicators other than the reaction test are simulated and labelled in the prototype. Blind Spot is not a clinical instrument or a diagnosis.

BEYOND SPACE

The same check could apply before safety-critical work on Earth: pilots before a flight, on-call medical staff, night shifts.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a framework; Supabase for anonymous data storage; Vercel for hosting; GitHub; three.js.
